entities.name: Henry IV, Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Henry IV, known as Henry the Elder, a prominent scion of the House of Welf, presided as Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg and ruling Prince of Wolfenbüttel from 1491 until his death on June 23, 1514. Born on June 24, 1463, his tenure spanned a pivotal period marking the transition from the late medieval era to the early modern age in the Holy Roman Empire, characterized by burgeoning dynastic conflicts, the rise of powerful territorial princes, and the initial tremors of the Reformation. His rule was significant for consolidating Welf power in a fragmented northern Germany, navigating complex imperial politics, and engaging in military campaigns that shaped the balance of power within the Lower Saxon Circle. He stands as a key figure in the intricate tapestry of German princely states during an epoch of profound transformation.

Upon his father William IV's death in 1491, Henry initially shared rule with his younger brother Eric I, but a division of territories in 1494 granted Henry sole control over the Principality of Wolfenbüttel, while Eric received Calenberg and Göttingen. A seasoned military commander, Henry distinguished himself in several conflicts, most notably as a key leader of the imperial forces during the Great Feud of the Saxon Brotherhood (Große Sächsische Fehde) from 1510 to 1514. This protracted conflict, primarily against the East Frisian Count Edzard I, saw Henry lead successful campaigns that secured the imperial ban against Edzard and resulted in the occupation of significant East Frisian territories, albeit temporarily. His military prowess was also evident in his participation in the campaigns against the rebellious Frisians under Duke Albert III of Saxony in 1500, and his service to Emperor Maximilian I in various imperial diets and military endeavors.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Henry IV's military leadership and political acumen solidified the Welf dynasty's regional power in northern Germany, particularly through his role in the Great Feud of the Saxon Brotherhood, which influenced the territorial integrity of the Principality of Wolfenbüttel for decades. His reign bridged the late medieval and early modern periods, contributing to the complex web of German princely states.
